title: The one who became many
hookLine: the week's story told whole: the one self becomes all
carry: the one self became all of us
tomorrow: 'I was Manu, and the sun.' a boast, or a fever?
last: TWO DOORS, ONE PLAIN I AM.

lines: SO YOU THINK YOU'RE A GOD?
cards: Three little words: aham, I; brahma, Brahman; asmi, am. A floormate reads them on a door sign and asks the obvious thing. So you think you're a god?
The honest answer is in the story this week has told in pieces. Today it's told whole, start to finish.

teach.b: In the beginning, the Brihadaranyaka says, there was only the self, in the shape of a person. It looked around, saw nothing but itself, and its first word was I am.
Then it was afraid, the way anyone alone in the dark is afraid, until it asked: there's nothing here but me, so what am I afraid of?
And the fear left, because fear comes from a second. But alone, it had no delight.
So it longed for a second, and split itself in two, and from that pair, the text says, people were born, and then every kind of creature in pairs, all the way down to the ants.
Then it knew: I am this creation, for I poured it all out of myself. And it entered everything it had become, to the tips of the fingernails, hidden like a razor in its case.
It's dearer than anything, because it's innermost.

teach.h: I AM BRAHMAN: IT BECAME ALL.
teach.b: And a few verses on, the text says it plainly: in the beginning this was Brahman, and it knew itself, I am Brahman, and so it became all. Here's the big teaching, plainly.
Most Vedanta teachers, Shankara and Ramanuja among them, read this as Brahman being both the maker of the world and what the world is made of.

The one became the many, and lives in each one as its self, its atman. That's why, as many teachers read it, aham brahmasmi isn't one person's boast. If it's true of me, it's true of the floormate asking, too.

how: In Advaita study, aham brahmasmi is learned in its Brihadaranyaka setting, word by word, with a teacher; other Vedanta schools read the 'I' in their own ways.

o: I bow to Brahman: a greeting at a temple
I study Brahman: a student's daily vow
I am Brahman: the self is the one reality

games.q: the whole story. tap the pairs.
p: it split in two and poured out all creatures
Brahman knew itself and became all

s: aham brahmasmi means 'my personality is God'
the I of the saying is the plain I said before any name, not the personality.
in the story, the self's fear left when it saw no second
fear comes from a second, the text says; seeing none, the fear left.
in this Upanishad, a maker builds the world out of some other stuff
the one self pours all creation out of itself and enters it; most Vedanta teachers read Brahman as both maker and material.

games.q: your little cousin asks: 'if God is in everybody, is God in the mean kid at school too?' by this week's story, what's honest?
o: yes: the one self became everyone, him too, even when he isn't acting like it.
no: only good people have the self inside them.
only priests and sages have Brahman in them.
games.why: in the Brihadaranyaka the one self became all and entered everything to the fingertips, and the saying is opened to gods, sages and people alike.

practice: Stand and take a slow walk, across the room and back. On one step think aham, on the next brahma, on the next asmi. On the way back, bring to mind the people nearby, one by one, and let the three words keep time for them too.
When you sit again, let them go.

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi: I am Brahman. Three small words, I, Brahman, am, and the whole story behind them: the one became the many.

orig.note: Sanskrit brahma, the form of Brahman inside the saying; joined to asmi, it becomes brahmasmi.

carryVoice: Your line: the one self became all of us. That's aham brahmasmi. A full week, well walked.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.1–8, 1.4.10 (the self alone says 'I am'; fear comes from a second; no delight alone; it falls into two, and from the pair come people and all creatures down to the ants; 'I am this creation, for I poured it forth from myself'; it entered here to the tips of the nails; dearer than all; aham brahmasmi)
Brahma Sutra 1.4.23 (prakritis ca: Brahman is the material cause as well as the maker), as Shankara and Ramanuja read it; Madhva's Dvaita school holds otherwise
